details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web application that compares landing locations and dates across nine Artemis III candidate regions near the lunar south pole. It answers a specific question: if we change the landing location or arrival date, how many hours of sunlight and direct-to-Earth communication do we gain or lose?

The tool combines NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides with real lunar terrain data collected by the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) aboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. For each site and every hour of 2028, it compares the positions of the Sun and Earth against the local horizon, accounting for terrain elevations that may obstruct them. The regions are defined using polygons published by USGS. Within each region, the project selects a representative point by evaluating sunlight availability and Earth visibility.

Users can compare up to four scenarios by adjusting the region, arrival date, and length of stay. The application displays sunlight hours, Earth visibility hours, and the longest continuous periods of darkness and direct communication outages. These results can be explored through timelines, a sky map, and a 3D scene featuring a 24 × 24-kilometer area of real terrain. It also includes a landing window calendar for 2028, CSV export, and shareable scenario links.

One of its creative features connects these data to an educational energy simulation: the lander’s solar panels track the Sun, its antenna points toward Earth, and its battery responds to lighting conditions. Depending on the available energy, the lander can operate, enter hibernation, or shut down. This allows users to understand visually how astronomical conditions and terrain barriers affect operations.

The main benefit is transforming specialized scientific data into understandable, comparable information. Its intended impact is to support STEM education, space outreach, and preliminary scenario exploration, introducing students, teachers, and the general public to the challenges of operating near the lunar south pole. The interface is available in Spanish and English and includes a guided tour to support classroom use.

We developed the application using TypeScript, React, and Vite; three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for 3D visualization; Node.js to download ephemerides; and Python, NumPy, and Pillow to process terrain data. We used Vitest for testing and GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions for deployment. Code and text were developed with assistance from Claude Code and ChatGPT/Codex and reviewed by the team.

During the design process, we considered the low elevation of the Sun and Earth above the horizon, terrain obstructions, continuity of power supply, communication outage duration, and interface clarity. We also explicitly state the limitations: terrain data have an 80-meter resolution, visibility is calculated geometrically, and eclipses, radio links, and relay satellites are not modeled. The energy simulation is intended for educational purposes, and the representative points selected by the application are not official landing sites.
